Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

randomPlantedForest (development version)

Breaking changes

  • rpf() has new defaults: a plain rpf(y ~ ., data) now returns the pruned model (class rpf_pruned), for regression and classification. The new defaults, each switched by its argument:
    • n_splits = NULL: the number of splits is chosen out of bag while the forest grows (was 30).
    • prune = NULL: the forest is pruned by prune_components() with its defaults, and every kept component of three or more predictors is shown in at most max_panels = 10 heat maps (was no pruning). With deterministic = TRUE it means prune = FALSE and n_splits = NULL means 30, as there are no out-of-bag rows.
    • n_try_split_points = NULL, share_candidates = NULL: 3 thresholds per candidate and 10% of the possible splits per round for split_structure = "leaf" (was 10 / 0.4, still the default of the other split structures). On 48 simulated and benchmark data sets this greediness had 5.7% to 6.8% lower test error than 10 / 0.4.
    • The split candidates of "leaf" are drawn by the fast draw (options(randomPlantedForest.exact_draw = FALSE), now the default): the same distribution as the exact draw, with other random numbers, so the same seed gives another forest. It is about 2.5 times as fast on larger data.
    • max_interaction = 3 (was 2). Order 3 had 15% lower test error than order 2 on simulated data and 1.5% on California housing; no limit (order p) was worse on California housing and 11 to 41 times slower.
    • n_families = 200 (was 50): more families had lower test error at every order (2% per doubling) and sparser pruned models. The loss is unchanged: "L2" for regression and "exponential" for classification (with more than two classes the multiclass exponential loss SAMME, see Bug fixes). So every default fit changes, regression and classification, and rpf() returns an rpf_pruned object instead of an rpf unless prune = FALSE. To fit a regression forest as before, give master’s settings and the exact draw:
    options(randomPlantedForest.exact_draw = TRUE)
rpf(..., max_interaction = 2, n_families = 50, n_splits = 30, n_try_split_points = 10, share_candidates = 0.4, prune = FALSE)
    Classification fits of earlier versions cannot be reproduced this way: they change for every split structure and loss (see Bug fixes: classification uses regression’s split structures, the largest value of a predictor can be split off, and three or more classes with the exponential loss use SAMME). The default call does more work than before: 0.2 s on mtcars, 0.4 s on iris, and about 2.3 minutes with a peak of 4.6 GB of resident memory (RSS; 2.7 GB of physical footprint, which varies by a few tenths of a GB from run to run) on California housing (16,512 rows) at 8 threads, measured with all changes of this version.

Renamed arguments

  • Four arguments of rpf() and the split structures have clearer names; the prefix gives the unit (n_ a count, share_ a share in (0, 1], max_ a cap):
    • ntrees → n_families (the number of tree families),
    • splits → n_splits (splits per tree family),
    • split_try → n_try_split_points (split points tried per candidate),
    • t_try → share_candidates (share of the possible splits drawn as candidates each round);
    • split_structure: "leaves" → "leaf", "hist" → "leaf_binned", "cur_trees_1" → "tree_then_leaf", "cur_trees_2" → "tree_then_all_leaves", "res_trees" → "target_tree_then_leaf" (the candidate, then how the leaf to split is found).
  • The old names still work and give the same fit, with a deprecation warning once per session for each old name (class lifecycle_warning_deprecated; options(lifecycle_verbosity = "warning") warns every time, "quiet" never); giving an argument under both names is an error. The same holds for oob_path_checkpoints(splits = ) and for a tune_control() ladder with the columns split_try and t_try.
  • The new names are used in print(), in the tables of the new features (the n_splits column of $oob_path, the tuning’s $tune$search and $tune$settings, greediness_ladder()), and in errors and documentation. A fitted model’s $params keeps the old names (ntrees, splits, split_try, t_try and the old split_structure values), so code that reads them, and models saved by 0.5.0, keep working.

New features

  • rpf() gains keep_level_order, to keep the level order of factor predictors instead of ordering their levels by the outcome. TRUE keeps it for every factor, ordered or not, and a character vector for the named factors only; splits then separate neighbouring levels in the order of levels(). The default, FALSE, orders every factor by the outcome as before, and fits are unchanged. The coding is stored in $factor_levels, which predict(), predict_components() and purify() use, and print() names the factors that keep their order. The details of ?rpf describe how factor predictors are coded.
  • plot() draws the trees of one tree family to illustrate how a Random Planted Forest predicts. type = "tree" draws a split diagram in the style of Figure 1b of the paper, reconstructed from the fitted leaves, type = "boxes" draws the leaves in variable space, before or after purification. rpf_boxes() returns the leaves as a data frame. Requires ggplot2, and patchwork for type = "boxes". The “Getting started” vignette uses it to show how a tree family is built and what purification does.
  • prune_components() prunes the purified components of a forest (regression or classification; see the classification entry below). A component is kept if its share of the variance of the prediction on the training rows is at least tau. Rule "D" drops the others; rule "R" also refits the intercept and one coefficient per kept component by least squares, which changes their scale but not their shape. The rule and tau are chosen out of bag by default (select_by = "oob"), without refitting: one purification evaluates every tree family’s components at the training rows outside its bootstrap sample, and each candidate is scored by its out-of-bag RMSE, corrected for the extra variance of averaging fewer families. On 52 data sets (44 synthetic, 8 splits of California housing) the out-of-bag choice picked the cross-validated model on 43, its test error was 0.09% higher on average, and it took a twelfth of the time. select_by = "cv" chooses by K-fold cross-validation instead, refitting the forest on each fold; by default it is used below 10 tree families and for deterministic forests. By default the largest tau whose error is within one standard error of the lowest is chosen (select = "1se"; select = "min" takes the lowest). With select_by = "oob", the coefficients of rule "R" are fitted on the out-of-bag components, to score each candidate, for the final model and for a given rule and tau, because the forest’s own components have also fitted the training rows’ noise; with select_by = "cv" they are fitted in sample. On the same 52 data sets this sparse default had 1.3% lower test error than the lowest out-of-bag error with in-sample coefficients, with half the components (29 instead of 83 on California housing) and no false component on the synthetic sets; it can drop a small true component (a four-way interaction in one synthetic design, +2.5% test error there). By default every kept component of three or more predictors is then shown in at most max_panels = 10 heat maps, and the model is pruned again with the shown components (max_panels = Inf switches this off). Two predictors of such a component stay at full resolution; the others are cut into intervals of equal numbers of training rows whose counts multiply to at most max_panels (a count of 1 averages a predictor out), the component is averaged within the cells (weighted by the product of the coarse predictors’ training marginals; the result is used as it is, not purified again), and the cuts that keep most of its variance are taken. The same rule then prunes again, so that the pruning judges the model that is shown; predictions use the coarsened components, and tau is then a share of that model’s variance. In simulations (48 data sets) this had 0.49% lower test error than coarsening after pruning, and 0.57% lower than not coarsening; on California housing (50 families, order 3) the default keeps 30 components, shown in 75 heat maps. Every fit records how often each training row is in each family’s bootstrap sample (fits are unchanged), and rpf_marshal(include_data = TRUE) stores these in-bag counts. On 44 synthetic data sets with known sparse structure, the pruned models kept no false component (except five tiny main effects on one additive set) and 111 of the 113 true interactions, and their test error was 15% lower than that of the unpruned forest tuned by CV, lower on 42 of the 44 sets. The result, of class rpf_pruned, has methods for predict(), predict_components() (now an S3 generic) and print(), and works with rpf_marshal(), rpf_unmarshal() and bundle().
  • rpf(oob_path = TRUE) gives the out-of-bag error along the splits from one fit, in $oob_path (for classification the loss’s criterion, see below). With the same seed, the forest with k splits is exactly the first k splits of a forest with more, so while each tree family grows, its prediction at the training rows outside its bootstrap sample is updated split by split. The table has the plain and the corrected out-of-bag RMSE (the correction of prune_components()) at four checkpoints per doubling of the splits (oob_path_checkpoints()), or at given ones. On 52 data sets, choosing n_splits by the lowest corrected error among the values of a cross-validation grid did as well as 5-fold cross-validation over that grid (test error 0.06% lower on average), at 0.9 of its cost. The fitted forest is the same as without oob_path, which is off by default.
  • rpf(n_splits = NULL) chooses the number of splits out of bag while the forest grows (regression and classification). The forest’s corrected out-of-bag error is followed at four checkpoints per doubling of the splits, growing stops once its lowest value is one doubling back (at most 25,600 splits), and the forest at the lowest error is returned: the forest that rpf() with that many n_splits and the same seed gives. On 52 data sets this chose the same n_splits as the lowest error along a fixed budget of 3,200 splits on 50, and a later, lower minimum on the other two, while growing 0.72 of the splits. The tree families grow one at a time, nthreads together, and keep only their out-of-bag predictions and a 40-byte record per split, from which the chosen forest is rebuilt without a refit; options(randomPlantedForest.adaptive_pause_gb) (1 GB) bounds the memory of families waiting for the stop. print() shows the chosen n_splits and where growing stopped. It is the new default (see Breaking changes). A corrected out-of-bag error at or below 0 at a checkpoint (a correction that overshot; never observed) is not chosen unless all are. A family waiting for the stop pauses at most one doubling past the first families’ estimate and grows on if the stop comes later, so a flat out-of-bag curve no longer makes every family grow far past the stop: a three-class fit with loss = "logit" and otherwise the defaults on 100 rows took 12 s instead of 35 s, with the same forest (measured when the pause was added, before the plateau stop below). Growing also stops once the error is on a plateau: once its lowest value has improved over the last doubling by at most one standard error of that improvement (paired over the training rows; options(randomPlantedForest.adaptive_tolerance), 1 by default, 0 for the stop on a new minimum alone). The choice is still the lowest error among the splits grown, so the plateau stop changes the forest only where the lowest error would have come later. On recorded paths it chose the same n_splits as the stop on a new minimum alone on all 44 synthetic regression sets, 4 splits of California housing and 24 classification fits (logit and exponential loss, binary and three classes), and grew 10% (regression) to 29% (classification) fewer splits. The families grow only to about the plateau stop (on 33 of these fits, 4 threads): the adaptive fit took 19% less time with logit, 4% less with the exponential loss, 11% less on 8 synthetic regression sets, and the same time on California housing, where the families waiting for the stop do not fit in the pause budget and grow on to the estimate of the stop on a new minimum, as a regrowth from their seed would cost more. A three-class fit on 100 rows with loss = "logit" and otherwise the defaults chooses 119 splits instead of 238 and takes 2.5 s instead of 8.7 s at 1 thread; with the default loss (exponential) it chooses 11 splits either way and stops growing at 15 instead of 21 (both measured with all changes of this version).
  • rpf(prune = TRUE) returns the pruned model instead of the forest (regression and classification): the forest is pruned by prune_components() with its defaults on the training rows, including the display at max_panels (a new argument of rpf(), 10 by default, Inf for no coarsening). The result equals prune_components(rpf(..., prune = FALSE), data) bit for bit from the same random number state, for the formula, x/y and recipe interfaces. With n_splits = NULL, one call chooses the number of splits out of bag, prunes and returns the model to show. prune = TRUE is an error with deterministic = TRUE, and purify is not used with it. It is the new default (prune = NULL, see Breaking changes); prune = FALSE returns the forest as before.
  • rpf() gains min_leaf_rows, the minimum number of rows on each side of every split, so in every leaf. Values above 1 need split_structure = "leaf" (for classification see below); the default 1 imposes no limit and is accepted everywhere. Leaves that cannot be split with this many rows on each side are no longer drawn as split candidates, and binary predictors are split whenever both sides keep enough rows. The default min_leaf_rows = 1 fits the same models as before, bit for bit.
  • Classification with split_structure = "leaf" (the default) takes min_leaf_rows and the fast draw of split candidates (options(randomPlantedForest.exact_draw = FALSE)) as regression does. Both use regression’s draw: the same candidates are left out, and a classification fit with loss = "L2" on a 0/1 response is the regression fit, bit for bit, with either option. With min_leaf_rows = 1 and the exact draw (the default before this version) classification fits are unchanged, bit for bit.
  • rpf(tune = TRUE) tunes out of bag in one call (regression and classification): the greediness of the split search (n_try_split_points and share_candidates, on the ladder of the new greediness_ladder()) and min_leaf_rows. Every forest of the search has n_splits chosen out of bag and is pruned by prune_components() with its defaults, and the forest whose pruned model has the lowest corrected out-of-bag error wins; the display (max_panels) is applied once, to the chosen model. The search is coordinate-wise, about 10 forests: the ladder from 10 / 0.4 to 1 / 0.0125, then min_leaf_rows 1, 5, 20 and 100, then the two ladder neighbours of the chosen point. tune = "quick" grows two forests, 3 / 0.1 and 1 / 0.025, and the new tune_control() sets your own search. The result is the chosen forest’s pruned model, with the search table in $tune. On 48 data sets (44 synthetic, 4 splits of California housing) the full search had 10.8% lower test error than 10 / 0.4 and 2.8% lower than 5-fold cross-validation over the same settings, at 1/24 of its cost; the quick preset had 9.4% lower test error. Those studies scored each forest with the pruning’s choice of the time (the lowest out-of-bag error, R’s coefficients in sample), not with the sparse default used here. The default stays tune = FALSE.
  • Classification forests go through the same pipeline as regression forests: rpf(oob_path = ), rpf(n_splits = NULL), prune_components() with its display (max_panels), rpf(prune = TRUE) and rpf(tune = ). Every out-of-bag choice is scored by the loss’s own criterion, corrected for the out-of-bag family count: for loss = "L1" and "L2" the squared error of the raw scores summed over the classes (the Brier score), for "logit" and "exponential" the log-loss of the probabilities that predict(type = "prob") returns, with the correction in its second-order form. On simulated data at 100 tree families the corrected out-of-bag log-loss was within -0.8% to +1.4% of the test log-loss (mean per setting), the uncorrected one +0.6% to +4.1% above it. A component is kept or dropped for all classes, sized by its variance summed over the score columns centred across the classes; rule "R" fits one coefficient per kept component, shared by the classes, and one intercept per score column (least squares for the Brier score, maximum likelihood for the log-loss), out of bag; the display chooses one panel form per component for all classes. The pruned model’s predict() takes type as predict.rpf() does, and its predict_components() has one column per component and class. With two classes and loss = "L2", every choice is that of the regression pipeline on the 0/1 response, bit for bit. With the new defaults (see Breaking changes) a classification fit takes all these steps.
  • options(randomPlantedForest.exact_draw = FALSE) draws the split candidates of regression with split_structure = "leaf" from a tree of weights kept up to date between rounds, instead of one random number per possible split in every round (?rpf, “The draw of candidates for leaves”). This fits about 2.5 times as fast on larger data, for example 218 s → 86 s at 1 thread on California housing (16,512 rows, max_interaction = 3, 10,000 splits). It draws from the same distribution and leaves out the same candidates under min_leaf_rows, but with other random numbers, so the same seed gives another forest. TRUE (the default before this version) fits the same models as before, bit for bit.
  • rpf() gains interaction_constraints, a list of feature sets that restricts which interactions the forest may form, as in xgboost: a tree on the predictors T is grown only if T is a subset of one of the sets. The sets are given by predictor names or column indices (with a formula, indices follow the formula’s predictors; with a recipe, names only). They apply together with max_interaction, for every split_structure, in regression and classification, and print() shows them. The default NULL leaves fits unchanged.
  • print() of a pruned model shows the final model: its intercept and its components, largest first, each with its importance, its share of the variance of the model’s prediction on the training rows ($components$model_share, a new column: the coefficient times the component, in the form the model uses, over the model’s prediction; for classification over the centred score columns). share, what tau thresholds, is the forest’s component before the coefficient: a three-predictor component of share 3.5% with coefficient 3.0 is 19% of the model. How the components were chosen (the forest’s families and splits, given or chosen out of bag, the rule and threshold, what was left out, the heat-map forms) follows under “How it was chosen”. No choice or fit changes.

Bug fixes

  • split_structure = "tree_then_leaf" samples leaves in proportion to their available thresholds, as documented. After a split, the sampling weights of new leaves counted rows instead of distinct values, and the cached prefix sums were built incorrectly. Leaves with tied values were then drawn too often, and draws were wasted on leaves that cannot be split. With deterministic = TRUE, "tree_then_leaf" evaluated only the first split candidate in every round; it now evaluates the first max_candidates, as the other split structures do. Fitted models change for regression with split_structure = "tree_then_leaf", random and deterministic.
  • split_structure = "target_tree_then_leaf" with deterministic = TRUE evaluates thresholds evenly spread over all (predictor, leaf, threshold) triples of a candidate. Previously it tried only the lowest thresholds of each leaf and left most of the variance unexplained. Fitted models change for regression with split_structure = "target_tree_then_leaf" and deterministic = TRUE only.
  • split_structure = "tree_then_all_leaves" with deterministic = TRUE evaluates n_try_split_points thresholds evenly spread over each leaf, as "tree_then_leaf" does. Previously it tried the 1st to 9th smallest values of each leaf. Fitted models change for regression with split_structure = "tree_then_all_leaves" and deterministic = TRUE only.
  • Classification’s split structures were never completed to match regression’s. They now use the same candidate pool, the same sampling of candidates, leaves and thresholds, and the same aging; only the loss differs. With loss = "L2" a classification fit on a 0/1 response now equals the regression fit (same seed). Previously "tree_then_leaf" was "tree_then_all_leaves"; "target_tree_then_leaf" used another candidate pool and ignored split_decay_rate; "leaf_binned" only ever split the root, so it fitted an additive model of stumps whatever max_interaction was; and "tree_then_all_leaves" never split the candidate tree’s own leaves. The fixes above for "tree_then_leaf" sampling and for deterministic = TRUE apply to classification too. Classification fits change for every split_structure and every loss.
  • The internal loss "exponential_2" no longer crashes.
  • Splits can separate the largest value of a predictor within a leaf. Previously every split structure except "leaf" for regression excluded that split, so binary predictors were never split on, and classification could not learn from them at all. Fitted models change for classification and for regression with split_structure other than "leaf".
  • A tree family that makes no split predicts the mean outcome of its bootstrap sample, and for classification its class shares (truncated to [epsilon, 1 - epsilon] with loss = "logit" or "exponential"). Previously it predicted 0, a probability of 0.5: constant predictors, a single row or min_leaf_rows above half the rows gave an all-zero model, and families that could not split pulled the forest towards 0. purify() puts that value into the intercept. Fitted models change only where a family made no split.
  • Errors while fitting or purifying with nthreads > 1 are reported as R errors. Previously an error in a worker thread terminated the R session.
  • predict(type = "link") works for classification forests with loss = "L1" or "L2". It returns the raw predictions, as type = "numeric" does (the link is the identity). Previously it stopped with an error about the size of pred.
  • rpf() stops with a clear error on inputs that gave wrong fits without a warning or failed later: an infinite outcome, epsilon outside (0, 0.5), delta of 0.5 or more (or 0 with loss = "logit"), t_try = 0, predictor names that are missing, duplicated or contain :, and interaction terms in the formula. rpf() finds interactions itself, so write y ~ x1 + x2 instead of y ~ x1 * x2; to fit a product as a predictor of its own, write I(x1 * x2) or add it to the data as a column. A character or logical outcome and a factor outcome with a single class get the package’s own message instead of one from hardhat or model.matrix(). Unused levels of a factor outcome are dropped with a warning; previously a binary outcome with an unused level was fitted, but predict() failed. predict() on zero rows returns zero rows instead of an error.
  • The C++ code compiles without warnings under -Wall -pedantic.
  • predict_components() returns one intercept per target level for multiclass classification, named by target_levels (#70). Previously only the first level’s intercept was returned, so components plus intercept did not sum to the prediction for other levels.
  • predict_components() accepts a matrix as new_data, like predict() does. It no longer turns the caller’s data.frame into a data.table by reference.
  • predict() after purify(maxp_interaction = k) with k below the fit’s max_interaction returns the forest’s prediction. Previously it returned the intercept plus the components up to order k, leaving out the higher orders. predict_components() now returns their sum as remainder, so that its result sums to the prediction, and rpf_marshal() keeps the purification’s cap.
  • loss = "exponential", the default for classification, is with more than two classes the multiclass exponential loss SAMME (Zhu, Zou, Rosset and Hastie, 2009): the split criterion, the leaf step and the weights all come from the one loss exp(-y.f / K). Each row has one weight, exp(-g) with g its class’s score, and a leaf moves the scores by log(p_k) - mean_j log(p_j), with p its weighted class shares (clamped as before by delta for the criterion and epsilon for the step); predict() takes the softmax of the scores as before. Previously each class had its own one-vs-rest weights, and its step was log(p_k / p_0) with p_0 = 1 - sum_k p_k mixing shares under the different weights; it is 0 at the start and was clamped to epsilon, so every class’s score rose by a common log(1 / epsilon) that the softmax ignores but the weights did not. The weights then no longer matched the probabilities predict() gives (by factors up to 10^10 in small tests). With n_splits chosen out of bag (n_splits = NULL) and the forest pruned (prune = TRUE; order 3, 200 families, n_try_split_points = 3, share_candidates = 0.1, the fast draw) on two simulated three-class data sets, the pruned model’s test log-loss was 0.022 and 0.036 above logit’s; it is now 0.061 below and 0.003 above, with 15 and 25 splits chosen instead of 21–25 and 238–400, and on the larger set (4,000 rows) the fit is four times as fast. Fitted models change for loss = "exponential" with more than two classes only; binary fits are unchanged.
  • purify() with mode = 2 no longer drops training rows that lie on a leaf’s lower bound. Purified components and the intercept now equal those of mode = 1.
  • predict_components() returns a remainder whenever m leaves out components of the forest, also when predictors leaves out some of the fit’s predictors at the fit’s max_interaction. Previously the intercept and m then did not sum to the prediction.
  • predict_components() takes the components’ predictors from the forest’s own columns, in their order. A formula with terms such as log(x1), I(x1^2) or . - x3 no longer makes it fail, and with factor predictors the components come in the order of the fit’s columns, which has the factors last.
  • predict_components() on a new_data with zero rows returns zero rows with the right columns, instead of failing with “Feature vector is empty.”.
  • print() counts the forest’s own predictor columns: with formula terms such as log(x1) or . - x3 it showed the number of raw columns the formula reads.
  • purify() on a forest purified with maxp_interaction = k purifies it again when asked for more orders (all orders by default). Previously it returned the forest unchanged, so the orders above k stayed zero in predict_components(). purify() also checks its arguments when the forest is already purified. A capped forest restored by rpf_unmarshal() without its training data cannot be purified again; asking for more orders is an error that says so.

Documentation

  • ?purify states how the components are identified (the marginal identification over the training rows, Hiabu, Meyer and Wright, 2023), and that the intercept is the mean prediction on the training rows.
  • ?rpf says that deterministic = TRUE also ignores split_decay_rate, how split_structure = "leaves" draws its thresholds, and that a seed reproduces a fit on the same platform only. splits counts rounds: near saturation a round can make no split. Ties between equally good candidates may go to different candidates under the exact and the fast draw, so their fits differ in distribution near saturation, though not in accuracy.
  • ?print.rpf_forest’s example prints a forest (export_forest = TRUE), and ?plot.rpf cites the RPF paper as 2020.

Performance

  • Classification with loss = "logit" fits 3x to 11x faster, with bitwise the same fits. For every candidate split, the logit loss copied the weights of all observations twice, although it reads only those of the leaf being split, so a candidate cost time in proportion to the sample size instead of the leaf size. With 300 rows and 150 splits (4 tree families, 1 thread), a binary fit takes 0.37 s instead of 1.9 s and a three-class fit 0.88 s instead of 2.9 s; with 1,000 rows and 500 splits, a binary fit takes 2.3 s instead of 26 s.
  • Fitting regression forests with split_structure = "leaf" (the default) is about 1.4 times as fast on larger data, for example 310 s → 216 s at 1 thread and 50 s → 34 s at 8 threads on California housing (16,512 rows, max_interaction = 3, 10,000 splits). Fitted models are bitwise unchanged.
  • predict() is about 3x faster for forests that are not purified, with bitwise the same predictions. From 512 rows on, each tree of more than 64 leaves gets an index of its leaves (a k-d tree, built per call), so a row is tested only against the leaves that may hold it instead of against every leaf. On California housing (100 tree families, max_interaction = 3, 4,128 rows) prediction takes 1.9 s instead of 5.7 s at 1 thread and 0.45 s instead of 1.26 s at 8 threads; with delete_leaves = FALSE, 2.9 s instead of 10.7 s and 0.71 s instead of 2.07 s.
  • Fitting regression forests with split_structure = "tree_then_leaf" is about 6 times as fast and needs less memory, for example 1,299 s → 216 s at 1 thread and 238 s → 38 s at 8 threads on California housing (16,512 rows, max_interaction = 3, 10,000 splits), with the peak memory at 8 threads down from 2.5 GB to 0.9 GB. Fitted models are bitwise unchanged.
  • purify() keeps the purified components as weighted rectangles instead of dense grids over all split points (with mode = 2, the default, which predict_components() and rpf(purify = TRUE) use). Purification at max_interaction = 3 and above no longer runs out of memory: on California housing (16,512 rows, 50 tree families, 94,138 leaves) order 3 takes 6 s and 0.25 GB with 4 threads, where it was stopped at 6 GB before, and the full order (8) takes 40 s and 2.3 GB. The components equal those of mode = 1 up to rounding, and rpf_marshal() stores the rectangles.
  • predict_components() evaluates all components in one pass over the rows of new_data, and skips those the forest does not hold, instead of one pass per component: on a 10-feature full-order fit (1,023 components, 636 of them not held), 5,000 rows take 0.5 s instead of 2.0 s.
  • prune_components(), and so rpf(prune = TRUE) and rpf(tune = ), no longer build the purified store of all components. Each tree family is purified in turn, its components are evaluated at the training rows (and out of bag) and then freed, and the pruned model stores the pieces of its kept components only, from which predict() and predict_components() evaluate them. purify() keeps every piece of every component, which grows steeply with the order: on California housing (16,512 rows, 200 tree families, n_try_split_points = 3, share_candidates = 0.1, the fast draw, 8 threads; both builds measured when this change was made) the whole call rpf(n_splits = NULL, prune = TRUE) at max_interaction = 8 (all predictors) was stopped at 12 GB of resident memory (RSS) while purifying, and now finishes with a peak physical footprint of 6.4 GB (9.9 GB RSS), most of it the coarsened components of the display; at order 3 the footprint peaks at 2.3 GB instead of 3.2 GB (RSS 4.1 GB instead of 5.4 GB), in the same time. The pruned models are the same up to rounding: on 136 pruned models of 36 forests (simulated and benchmark data, orders 2 to 10) the choices, the kept components and the display are the same, and test predictions agree to 3e-15 of their scale. The forest in the result is left unpurified (call purify() for all its components), and an earlier purification of it is no longer redone.
  • A fitted forest takes about 40% less memory: the split search’s per-leaf caches are kept apart from the leaves and freed when a tree family is finished, so a leaf takes 80 instead of 232 bytes; finished classification forests now also drop their training rows and caches. On California housing (max_interaction = 3, 10,000 splits, 200 tree families) the fitted forest falls from 821 MB to 490 MB and the fit’s peak resident memory from about 1.9 GB to 1.6 GB, in the same time. Fitted models are bitwise unchanged.
  • Classification with loss = "logit" fits another 1.2x to 1.8x faster, with bitwise the same fits. The terms of the loss under the current weights do not depend on the candidate split, so each observation’s terms are now computed once and refreshed only when its weights change, and the terms of classes the observation is not in (which are zero) are skipped: a candidate takes one exponential per logit column and one logarithm per observation of the leaf, instead of two exponentials and two logarithms per column plus two logarithms. With 4,000 rows, 300 splits, 200 tree families and max_interaction = 3 (1 thread), a binary fit takes 74 s instead of 95 s and a three-class fit 91 s instead of 129 s; with 300 rows, 8.8 s → 6.2 s (binary) and 22.5 s → 13.6 s (three classes).

randomPlantedForest 0.5.0

Breaking changes

  • rpf() now defaults to max_interaction = 2, main effects and pairwise interactions, instead of 1, an additive model (#66). Values above the number of predictors are capped silently instead of with a message.
  • rpf() now defaults to loss = "exponential" for classification instead of "L2", so classification fits give proper probability estimates by default; regression still uses "L2" (#66).
  • rpf() arguments are reordered by purpose (forest size, split search, loss, other). Pass arguments after the data arguments by name (#66).
  • rpf(), predict() and purify() error on unknown arguments, such as misspelled ones, instead of silently ignoring them (#66).
  • purify() is a regular function instead of an S3 generic (#66).
  • preprocess_predictors_predict() is no longer exported; it is an internal step of predict() (#66).
  • The package now requires R >= 4.1.0 (#66).
  • For a given seed, classification models differ from 0.4.0 due to the fixes and speedup below, but regression models are unchanged (#57, #66).
  • For direct users of the C++ object ($fit): set_data() no longer fits, call fit() afterwards, and an unknown classification loss is an error instead of a silent fallback to L2 (@jyliuu, #57).
  • rpf() no longer has a cv argument, which never had an effect: the C++ cross-validation was a no-op (#66).

Bug fixes

  • predict() and predict_components() error on missing values in new_data, naming the affected columns. Previously such rows silently received arbitrary predictions, as rpf() has no handling for missing values. rpf() likewise reports missing values in the training data by column (#66).
  • Classification fits with a fixed seed could differ between runs. When a split replaced a leaf, its new split candidates could be lost or attached to the wrong leaf, depending on memory layout (#66).
  • predict(type = "class") breaks probability ties by level order instead of at random, so class predictions are deterministic and no longer advance the random number generator (#66).
  • purify() returns its input invisibly, as documented (#66).
  • Logical predictors in the formula interface are used as a single 0/1 column, as in the x/y interface. Previously they were expanded into two redundant indicator columns, which also counted against max_interaction (#66).

Performance

  • Prediction is much faster: leaves are scanned from flat, cache-friendly arrays (~15x single-threaded), and rows are split across threads (#65). predict() gains nthreads, defaulting to the nthreads used for fitting.
  • predict_components() is much faster: purified forests look up only the trees of the requested component, and each distinct input row is predicted once, which pays off for low-cardinality features (#59, #65).
  • Classification fits are slightly faster, as redundant work during model construction was removed (#57).

Other improvements

  • New “Getting started” vignette covering regression, classification, component decomposition, recipes, and saving models (#66).
  • The print() method is overhauled and gains a format() counterpart: it reports the forest size, interaction degree, purification state, split search settings and number of threads (#66).
  • deterministic = TRUE with ntrees > 1 warns, as all tree families are then identical (#66).
  • Rewritten documentation for rpf(), purify() and predict_components(), including guidance on choosing parameters and on how purification interacts with predict_components() (#66).

Internals

  • The C++ core no longer depends on Rcpp: it uses standard C++ types and exceptions, and an Rcpp layer (src/rcpp_interface.*) converts at the boundary. This is groundwork for bindings in other languages such as Python (@jyliuu, #57).
  • cli and rlang are now imported, mvtnorm is only needed to build the pkgdown site (#66).

randomPlantedForest 0.4.0

It is now possible to serialize and de-serialize an rpf object via marshalling, meaning a fitted model can be saved to disk or dispatched to a worker process for parallelization or encapsulation, as is done in mlr3. This also re-opens the door for the mlr3extralearners wrapper, which was removed due to the lack of serialization support.

  • New rpf_marshal() / rpf_unmarshal() serialize a fitted forest to a plain R list and back, making saveRDS()-based storage of rpf models possible (#52). Purified forests restore their purified state directly; training data is only embedded with include_data = TRUE (required to purify() after restoring). Blobs record the blob format version and the package version they were created with; restoring under an older package than the one that saved the model warns. Malformed or corrupt blobs error instead of reading out of bounds.
  • New rpf_is_valid() checks whether an rpf object’s internal model is usable, predict(), purify() and predict_components() now give an actionable error for rpf objects restored via readRDS() without marshaling.
  • New bundle::bundle() method for rpf models wrapping the marshaling API.

Behavior changes

  • The default for delta changed from 0 to 0.001. With delta = 0, splits producing single-class nodes have infinite logit loss and are always rejected, which also degraded binary logit fits.

Fixes and improvements

  • Fixed multiclass classification with loss = "logit", which effectively never split and predicted near-uniform class probabilities (#40). The C++ logit loss is a reference-class multinomial formulation expecting K-1 indicator columns, but the R wrapper passed a full K-column one-hot matrix, pinning the implicit reference-class probability to zero. Multiclass logit outcomes are now encoded with the first factor level as reference class:
    • predict(type = "prob") reconstructs all K class probabilities from the K-1 logits; rows sum to 1 exactly.
    • predict(type = "numeric"/"link") now returns K-1 columns named after the non-reference levels (previously K columns).
    • predict_components() on multiclass logit fits returns per-class components for the K-1 non-reference levels; target_levels reflects this.

randomPlantedForest 0.3.0

Major changes (#61)

  • New rpf() arguments controlling split-candidate sampling:
    • split_structure = "leaves": Defines what a split candidate is and how candidates are drawn. One of "leaves" (default), "hist", "cur_trees_1", "cur_trees_2", or "res_trees"; see ?rpf for details.
    • max_candidates = 50: Maximum number of split candidates sampled per iteration.
    • split_decay_rate = 0.1: Exponential aging of repeatedly drawn but unchosen split candidates. split_decay_rate = 0 corresponds to no aging and uniform sampling.
    • delete_leaves = TRUE: Whether a parent leaf is deleted when splitting along an existing dimension.
  • Fitting results change: The new candidate-sampling defaults and a reworked internal RNG mean that fits are not reproducible against previous versions, even with the same seed. Install an older commit if exact reproduction of previous results is required.
  • Seeded fits are now reproducible regardless of nthreads: per-tree seeds are drawn from R’s RNG, so set.seed() gives identical forests for serial and multithreaded fits.
  • Substantial speedups in fitting (cached per-leaf orderings, prefix sums) and reduced memory use (training-only buffers are released after each tree family is built).
  • purify() gains arguments:
    • mode = 2: Purification algorithm; 2 is a new fast exact method, 1 is the legacy grid-based path.
    • nthreads = NULL: Purification is now multithreaded, defaulting to the fit’s nthreads setting.
    • maxp_interaction = NULL: Optionally only compute purified components up to this interaction order.
  • New rpf() argument export_forest = FALSE: The flattened forest is no longer stored in the fitted object by default, so rpf_object$forest is NULL unless export_forest = TRUE. This reduces object size; predict(), purify(), and predict_components() are unaffected.
  • preprocess_predictors_predict() is now exported.
  • Fixed a memory bug in the legacy purification path where the grid was sized one element too large, causing out-of-bounds reads (crashes on Windows, silently wrong purification results elsewhere).
  • Fixed a crash on Windows when fitting with nthreads > 1, caused by a thread_local buffer with a non-trivial destructor being destroyed at thread exit.

Other changes

  • Internals in src/ have been refactored into modular sub-files (#53)
  • rpf() now errors if a regression target is combined with a loss other than "L2".
  • Allow features of type logical, which are now converted via as.integer.
  • The parallel = TRUE|FALSE argument in rpf() has been substituted by an nthreads = 1L argument, allowing for more flexible parallelization. The previous behavior only allowed for either no parallelization or using n-1 of n available cores. The new implementation should be reasonably robust and the default behavior remains serial execution.
  • Remove SystemRequirements field from DESCRIPTION: Now the default C++ version is C++17 and with a minor change to internal use of random numbers, randomPlantedForest is now compatible with C++11 through C++23.
  • Add remainder term to predict_components output for case where max_interaction supplied is smaller than max_interaction in rpf fit. In that case, the m values don’t sum up to the global predictions, so we add a remainder to allow reconstruction of that property.

randomPlantedForest 0.2.1

  • Add glex class to output of predict_components(), for extended functionality available with glex.
  • Add target_levels vector to output of predict_components() to aid multiclass handling. Keeping track of levels is somewhat awkward since column names of $m need to be identifiable regarding the target level.

randomPlantedForest 0.2.0

  • Added a NEWS.md file to track changes to the package.
